clue.text: Dreaming, so crashes into gorge

indicators.note: things that crash end up broken and jumbled, so the letters of the first two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A daydreamer, lost in thought, walks straight into a ravine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gorge' looks like a ravine the dreamer falls into, but it is the verb: to eat greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are verbs for eating greedily and to excess; the longer one is a variant spelling of gourmandise.

clue.text: His song about J Eccles is grind

definitions.meaning: the Hollies' 1968 hit 'Jennifer Eccles' was co-written by Graham Nash, so the songwriter's initial plus surname is meant
to grind the teeth together, as in anger

explanation.surface: Someone's song about a person called J Eccles is said to be dreary.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is Eccles, so the clue seems to be about him; 'Jennifer Eccles' is a 1968 pop song by The Hollies, written by Allan Clarke and Graham Nash, whose initial and surname run together give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Grinding the teeth in rage or pain is exactly the action of this verb; synonym.

clue.text: Take back ownership from theological study group on ship

parts.note: RE is religious education, the school subject
a posse is a band of people gathered for a purpose
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A ship's religious study circle has its property seized.
explanation.definitionFit: When a lender seizes goods back from a defaulting buyer, it reclaims title to them; a synonym phrase.

clue.text: Maybe fan of song by One Direction desperately short of energy

indicators.note: by means next to, so the song sits beside what follows

parts.note: an air is a tune or song

indicators.note: done desperately means done wildly and in disarray, so the band's name is rearranged
short of means lacking, so the letter for energy is dropped from the band's name

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A devoted follower of a boy band song is in a desperate, exhausted state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fan' reads as a pop devotee of One Direction, but it is a cooling device; 'desperately' rearranges ONE DIRECTION once 'short of energy' has removed one E.
explanation.definitionFit: An electric fan is one example of a machine for cooling a room, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: 22 study a raisin, oddly

parts.note: a den is a private room for work or study

indicators.note: taking the odd-numbered letters of the dried grape, first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: A cross-reference to another answer, followed by a study of a raisin's odd features.
explanation.walkthrough: '22' points to the answer of 22-down, COINS, which is the definition here.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman silver pieces of money, so they are examples of the other answer, the change in your pocket.

clue.text: Originated from tourists in Cornwall being up before the first sign of daylight

indicators.note: before puts the reversed tourists ahead of the next letter
in a down clue, up means the word is written from the bottom, i.e. backwards

parts.note: emmets is Cornish dialect for tourists (literally ants)

indicators.note: takes the opening letter of the word daylight

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers in Cornwall are up before dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Cornwall is a county in south-west England where locals call visitors EMMETS; 'being up' turns it into STEMME in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem from something is an idiom for arising or coming from it, as a branch grows from its trunk.

clue.text: Legal age to host party?

indicators.note: the two words play host to the letters, which sit inside them across the word break

explanation.surface: A question about the legal age for throwing a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive celebration or special occasion, so it is a kind of festivity or bash.

clue.text: Sometimes, one works without clothes?

parts.note: a performer on stage or screen occasionally has to appear naked for a role

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a naturist's job description; it describes a stage or film performer, who now and then plays nude scenes.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre and film performers sometimes play naked scenes, which is the cryptic description given.

clue.text: Contract spy regarding those people briefly being detained

indicators.note: being detained means held inside, so the short words are held within the spy

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy
re means about or regarding
'em is a shortened them

explanation.surface: A spy is under contract concerning some people who are being held.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a verb to go with the spy, but it is the noun for a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: A contract is a binding deal or pact between parties, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Unrelated songs broadcast as fillers?

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered about, as seed is sown, so the letters are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: Random songs put out on the radio to fill airtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fillers' reads as radio padding, but it means people who fill teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Dentists put fillings into decayed teeth, so they are whimsically the ones who fill; a cryptic sense.

clue.text: Ambitious German discarded drug

indicators.note: discarded means thrown away, so the letter for German is taken out

parts.note: aspiring means ambitious, hoping to rise

explanation.surface: An ambitious German gave up drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A common painkiller, acetylsalicylic acid, so an example of a medicine.

clue.text: Competitor always seizes opening

indicators.note: seizes means grabs and holds, so the word for always clasps the opening inside it

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
a vent is an opening or outlet

explanation.surface: A rival who always grabs the chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'always' is the poetic contraction, not the four-letter EVER, which leaves a letter too many.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider in horse trials (dressage, cross-country, jumping) is a contestant in equestrian sport.

clue.text: That man's getting Robbie, perhaps, to lie about plot

parts.note: his means belonging to that man

indicators.note: to lie about means to be turned round, so the actress's first name is read backwards

parts.note: Margot Robbie is an Australian actress, so Robbie is one example of someone with this first name

explanation.surface: A man gets Robbie Williams, perhaps, to fib about a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robbie' suggests the singer Robbie Williams; the name needed is the actress Margot Robbie, with 'to lie about' turning MARGOT into TOGRAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar chart showing frequencies is a kind of statistical graph, which one can call a plot.

clue.text: Short Peter Sellers covers

indicators.note: the comedian's name covers the letters, holding them inside across the space

explanation.surface: Peter Sellers records brief cover versions of songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Sellers was a British comic actor; 'covers' looks like cover songs but means the name contains the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Curt and brief in speech or writing; a direct synonym for being brusquely concise.

clue.text: Reportedly reproduced money

indicators.note: reportedly means as said, so the word for reproduced is heard rather than seen

parts.note: bred means produced offspring

explanation.surface: Money is said to have multiplied.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for cash, as in earning one's crust; an informal synonym.

clue.text: Some Czechs in Bosnia working to protect border

indicators.note: to protect means to surround and shelter, so the rearranged letters wrap round the border
working means in operation or reworked, so the country's letters are rearranged

parts.note: a hem is the edge or border of cloth

explanation.surface: Some Czech workers in Bosnia guard a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is only a link; the rearranged country letters split around the border after their first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: People of Bohemia, a historic region of the Czech Republic, are a subset of Czechs.

clue.text: No decline should be misconstrued as laziness

indicators.note: misconstrued means wrongly interpreted, so the two words are rearranged into another reading

explanation.surface: A warning that refusing to go down should not be mistaken for idleness.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are nouns for idleness and an unwillingness to work; synonym.

clue.text: Are fusion bombs immoral?

indicators.note: bombs means explodes, blowing the letters apart into a new order

explanation.surface: A moral question: are hydrogen bombs wicked?
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked or villainous, a near synonym for morally bad behaviour.

clue.text: He said I inhaled, but was reluctant

indicators.note: inhaled means breathed in, so I goes inside the word for said

parts.note: stated means said

explanation.surface: A politician admits he smoked, but grudgingly, echoing a famous evasive denial.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes Bill Clinton's 'I didn't inhale'; here 'inhaled' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To pause or falter before acting is to show reluctance; synonym phrase.

clue.text: 18 down tools, primarily supported by the French, to get Scottish representation

indicators.note: in a down entry the supporting piece sits below, so the French article comes last

parts.note: the clue refers to itself, so it means this

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take the opening letter of tools

parts.note: le is French for the

explanation.surface: Workers down tools to secure Scottish representation, backed by the French.
explanation.walkthrough: '18 down' is this very clue, so it gives THIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The prickly plant is Scotland's national emblem, so it stands for that country.

clue.text: Forced to serve doctor and American newspaper editor

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper

explanation.surface: A doctor and an American newspaper editor are pressed into service.
explanation.definitionFit: Conscripted into the armed forces, as in the US call-up; synonym.

clue.text: Out of shape individual enthrals female

indicators.note: enthrals means holds captive, so the single thing holds the letter for female inside

parts.note: a unit is a single thing, an individual

explanation.surface: A flabby man captivates a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Not in good physical condition; a synonym phrase.

clue.text: Still on a plane? That's very masculine!

definitions.meaning: Mach 0, a speed of zero as a Mach number, describes an aircraft at a standstill

explanation.surface: Pilots' joke: standing still in a jet is a manly thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Mach numbers measure aircraft speed against the speed of sound, so Mach zero, written with an O, is no speed at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing aggressive pride in manliness; a synonym for overtly masculine.

clue.text: Business in strife, initially, resulting in change

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so take the opening letter of strife

explanation.surface: A company in trouble starts to change.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose change is the metal money in your pocket; synonym.

clue.text: Maiden wearing Russian flower around August

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the month's abbreviation sits inside

parts.note: in means wearing, as in 'in a hat'
a flower in crosswords is a river, something that flows; the Ural is a river in Russia

explanation.surface: A young woman wears a Russian flower in late summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' looks like the woman wearing the flower, but it means first, as in a maiden voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden voyage or speech is the first of its kind, as is an opening or first one.

clue.text: Nothing tops lying around swimming pools

indicators.note: lying around means placed surrounding, so the tops enclose the zero

parts.note: lids are tops of containers
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Bikini tops left lying around the pool area.
explanation.definitionFit: Public open-air bathing places, especially in Britain, are pools of this sort; synonym.

clue.text: Fifty advanced in disorder to get food

indicators.note: advanced means moved forward, so the letter for fifty moves to an earlier place

parts.note: an ailment is an illness or disorder
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Fifty people move forward in chaos to get something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorder' looks like an anagram signal, but it is an illness; 'advanced' moves its L one place forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal word for nourishment or sustenance; synonym.

clue.text: Start to taste whisky from long ago, getting double

indicators.note: start of means the opening letter, so take the first letter of taste

parts.note: W is Whisky in the NATO phonetic alphabet
of old means from long ago

explanation.surface: Tasting an old whisky and asking for a double.
explanation.definitionFit: Twice as much, or in two parts; a direct synonym for double.

clue.text: Very small entrance to office is just about adequate

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so good'

indicators.note: the entrance to a word is its first letter, here of office

explanation.surface: A tiny office doorway is barely good enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Mediocre, neither good nor bad; a synonym for passable.

clue.text: George stops flat-earther's nemeses?

parts.note: desists means stops

explanation.surface: George puts an end to his enemies' belief in a flat earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat-earther's nemeses' is a playful definition: scientists who measure the shape of the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Scientists who measure the earth's size and curved shape would refute anyone claiming it is flat.
